name: Korean→English Medical Interpreting Drill
_note: Skill drill. Standard metric keys re-pitched: medical_accuracy = meaning fidelity to the Korean source, clinical_reasoning slot = register switching (patient-friendly vs chart English), communication_fluency = speed and naturalness of the rendition.

anchors.90-100: Renditions sound like a native clinician; no Korean-influenced word order or article errors
anchors.70-80: Occasional minor errors; renditions always sound natural enough
anchors.50-60: Understandable but noticeably literal or Korean-influenced phrasing
anchors.30-40: Frequent literal translation; listener must reconstruct the meaning
anchors.10-20: Renditions are largely word-for-word and hard to follow

anchors.90-100: Every rendition preserves the full clinical meaning of the Korean source — symptoms, time course, doses, qualifiers
anchors.70-80: Meaning preserved; rare omission of a minor qualifier
anchors.50-60: Core meaning kept but details (duration, frequency, severity) sometimes dropped
anchors.30-40: Renditions distort or omit clinically important content

anchors.90-100: Consistently picks the right register — plain English to patients, clinical register for chart/handover lines
anchors.70-80: Mostly correct register; occasional jargon to a patient or casual wording in a handover
anchors.50-60: One register used for everything; sometimes inappropriate

anchors.90-100: Starts the English version promptly and delivers it smoothly in one go
anchors.70-80: Brief hesitation, then a fluent rendition
anchors.50-60: Noticeable pauses and restarts but completes the rendition
anchors.10-20: Unable to produce a rendition without heavy prompting

anchors.90-100: Stays composed on hard items; asks for repetition professionally; self-corrects gracefully
anchors.70-80: Generally composed; recovers well from misses
anchors.50-60: Some flustering on misses but keeps going
anchors.10-20: Gives up on items without attempting

checklist.item: rendered a patient symptom statement with the time course preserved (e.g. 'for three days')
rendered a medication instruction with dose/frequency intact (e.g. 'twice a day, after meals')
used patient-friendly plain English for at least one doctor-to-patient instruction
used clinical register for at least one chart/handover line (e.g. 'a 65-year-old man with a history of…')
asked for repetition or clarification in English when needed, instead of going silent
self-corrected a literal/Konglish phrasing into a natural one
